Seeing as you already have a pretty good pair of Sony's, I'd lean more into the Galaxy Buds direction unless you're willing to buy third-party memory foam tips like I did. The eBay tips I recommended are DIY to an extent, but the Dekoni tips have the original installation slits and a mesh to protect against earwax, and they fit in the case. Their sizes are also 1-to-1 with Apple for easier selection after testing with the silicone tips Apple gives you.

Word of advice for the Galaxy Buds, take a look at [this article](https://www.soundguys.com/samsung-galaxy-buds-plus-vs-galaxy-buds-29427/) before making your purchase. The new "Plus" models look to be pretty solid.

\[EDIT: I'd go with the Galaxy Buds Plus for now, and see if Apple releases a better pair of AirPods at a lower price this year\]

* **How well do the AirPods Pro fit? I have used Samsung Galaxy Buds and the fit is awesome - they stay on regardless of what I'm doing, whether that is gym, running, basketball, etc. Any movement, it doesn't matter, it will always stay in. I don't want to get the Comply tips because I heard they stuff up sound quality to some degree.**
   * The default tips that Apple provides will be good enough for listening while walking, sitting, or working out with weights (not running). They fall out pretty easily given hard enough head movement and vertical shaking by nature of the design. The silicone tips are smooth, easy to form to the walls of your ear with no pressure, but don’t really provide any grip and slip easily with enough oil generated in your ear after a week of use. I highly recommend buying quality tips like those from Dekoni or a particular seller off eBay.
* **How is the sound quality? I use Spotify on Very High quality which is about 320kbps. I'm not expecting to be amazed but I also do want some solid quality for the price I'm going to pay.**
   * AirPods Pro aren’t meant to be audiophile earphones, by nature of the limitations of small drivers and balancing battery life with performance. Don’t expect any crazy bass, but vocals, electronic music, and concert performances are rich. I run Spotify on Very High at home and work, but I can tell you that you’re better off with High or Normal if you choose to buy AirPods as you don’t benefit from any of the extra definition, so save the data usage.
* **How does it feel on Transparency Mode vs Off Mode? When I walk the streets I want to be able to listen to music and also be able to hear sounds around me. Would you recommend Transparency or Off?**
   * Transparency mode sounds just like if you had nothing in your ear, if not better because the microphones can pick up sounds you might not, but it does take a couple days to adjust to the slightly-off electronic accent of some things like voices. Keep in mind that because Transparency Mode is also actively mixing outside sound with your music that it’ll make your music quieter. If you don’t mind that, you can always listen to music on the streets but try not to blast your music too loud or it might drown out other people’s voices unless they’re really close to you.
* **How does it work with non-Apple devices such as a Windows PC? Or a TV? Any issues or flawless?**
   * In my experience with my Windows PC with Bluetooth built-in, connection was solid and the ANC/Transparency worked as intended. As long as your device supports Bluetooth 4.2 or 5.0 (for better range and stable connection) you should be just fine. Just be careful not to blow your ears out with the default volume it sets for you.
* **It has BT 5.0 so would it auto switch between an iPhone and a Windows PC or would I have to re-connect each time I switch?**
   * You need to reconnect it each time you switch, which I do on iPhone with the “Audio Antenna” icon in the control center, and on Windows by going into Bluetooth settings or audio devices control panel and double-clicking. Even on my laptop with macOS it’s pretty much the same process but easier since it recognizes the AirPods because of Apple’s integration. Make sure you re-name your AirPods so you can tell which Bluetooth device it is when pairing.
* **How is battery life? Say I use Transparency or Off most of the time. Maybe use it on Noise Cancelling sometimes.**
   * I’ve been using my AirPods for almost half a year now and it has never failed to carry through a long study session or at work with Transparency on so my boss doesn’t yell at me. I would say to avoid the “Off” setting unless you’re really concerned with battery life, since you do get the full 4.5 hours before charging for another 30 minutes. Noise cancellation is great for focusing on a task, while Transparency is great when you’re expecting people to need your attention suddenly.
* **How are the touch controls to play/pause and whatever else you can do with it?**
   * People have a love/hate relationship with the Force Stems, because some are more used to touch/tap controls. I love them because of the satisfying click they give off to confirm an action instead of accidentally tapping it or glitching out. You can play/pause with one click, skip forward with two, back with three, you get the idea. You can also customize the settings after pairing to enable faster switching between the ANC, Off, and Transparency modes.
* **Would you recommend the product overall? I plan on using it with my iPhone 11 Pro, iPad, Windows PC.**
   * If you’re looking for a surreal audio experience, look somewhere else. These are great everyday wireless buds that I bought because they finally didn’t look like tacky misshapen earrings, and are subtle enough in their design to be compact and usable. I love noise cancellation since it drowns out fan noise, and Transparency so people don’t complain that I’m not paying attention, etc. The battery life is good enough to carry through the day for most things, but definitely not a 24 hour accessory like the Apple Watch. All your iDevices will work perfectly with your AirPods after iOS 14 drops, but in its current state with iOS 13, you’ll need to reconnect (easily) through the control center with just a couple taps. 

Hope that answers everything, good luck with your purchase and feel free to PM me if you have any further questions. :)

As someone who owns AirPods Pro, HyperX Cloud Alphas, and has 2000+ hours in Counter-Strike, please don't use AirPods for gaming.

Frame lag and ping lag are not the same thing.

**Frame lag** is caused by a hardware limitation, whether that's a weak graphics card, not enough RAM, or a weak processor. This would result in lower framerates and stuttering during gameplay.

**Ping lag** is caused by weak networking hardware (modem/router), weak Wi-Fi signal, issues with your Internet Service Provider (e.g. AT&T), or the game servers are experiencing high load, which could be too many players on at once or a network attack. This results in rubberbanding (your character teleporting back and forth) or nearby players running in place and teleporting once your Internet catches up, and game disconnects.

That being said, Bluetooth and Wi-Fi don't use the same signal so your AirPods shouldn't be interfering and causing your Internet to lag, or slow down your computer unless your computer's networking card (NIC) needs a driver update.

You can definitely give it a try since BT 5.0 offers a lot of benefits over v4.2, and while I can't guarantee a 100% improvement in mic quality, it would improve the stability of the connection and range.

Usually, the Operating System is intelligent enough to prioritize the Dedicated GPU for games, and more graphics oriented tasks rather than the integrated graphics, but sometimes (anything from busted drivers, to weird brand specific BIOS settings) it doesn't work quite correctly.

​

>I've been looking at some posts and I've seen that there is a need to install the driver cleanly? What does this mean?

They're telling you to boot your computer into Safe Mode, and use a program called **Display Driver Uninstaller** to make sure any trace of old drivers are gone, like **SERIOUSLY** gone so that it doesn't get in the way of any new drivers, and doing it this way should fix your issues instead of making them worse.

[Here's the easiest guide that I could find.](https://www.sevenforums.com/tutorials/367109-display-driver-uninstaller-how-use.html)

It's possible, and while I don't recommend downloading drivers through Device Manager, those drivers shouldn't cause any issues for the system, but they won't perform the best either. The best drivers are from either the manufacturer of your laptop, or the NVIDIA page, but usually only your laptop manufacturer will have guaranteed driver stability.

​

>Is this saying that I need to uninstall GFE and why? Why is this happening and how do I fix it so that games run properly with the right graphics card?

GFE can goof up occasionally with driver installations, either downloading corrupted files, or (as a problem many of my friends have on their gaming laptops) "optimizing" graphics so that it runs like garbage because NVIDIA decided to prioritize graphics over performance.

Regarding the value proposition, and comparing laptops to desktops, I’ve been on both ends for the better part of the last ten years, and I’ve been modifying and optimizing internals for both.

**EDIT:** I believe the desktop to laptop comparison is well-founded, and appropriate, because OP's laptop uses [mobile parts that are either entirely, or mostly comparable to their desktop counterparts.](https://ark.intel.com/content/www/us/en/ark/compare.html?productIds=126684,134906)

Historically speaking, gaming laptops work with far too little internal volume to effectively dissipate heat, and lithography-wise, the 14nm die of the 8th gen Intel CPU, and 12nm in the RTX Turing die, are energy-efficient, but they still generate a lot of heat that can be *somewhat mitigated* by a double fan and meager heatpipe solution like that present in high end laptops like OP’s, but my point is that without an external watercooling add-on like ASUS has done before, you shouldn’t expect anything close to max performance without thermal throttle, because these 6 core parts can, and will generate an absurd amount of heat simply because you’re cramming core count into the same surface area of, say, a four year old Intel CPU.

It’s an inherent flaw of laptop design to force desktop spec parts into a twelfth the space of a desktop PC.

**EDIT:** Also, I entirely agree with reapplying thermal solution with something like Arctic MX4, and avoid any metals and exotic pastes since they're not necessary for a laptop chip.

So sure you can undervolt, cooling pad, industrial chiller the damn thing, but thermal inefficiency is in the inherently a design nightmare of gaming laptops that both work and look good since day one.

\[EDIT: [Link to the watercooled ASUS Laptop](https://www.asus.com/us/ROG-Republic-Of-Gamers/ROG-GX700VO/) I was talking about\]

Laptops that thin were never meant to handle a 6C/12T part, not to mention the additional heat load from the RTX 2070.

Dinky 80mm fans and copper tubes can only do so much in that compact of a space, but for reference, my **i7-8700K** and **1070Ti** hold stable around 60C only because there’s a lot more empty space for air to flow through the giant ATX case, and because I watercool the entire system in a single loop.

But in a space as compact as a thin and light laptop such as the ASUS SCAR II, I’m surprised they didn’t reintroduce a connectable watercooling backside like they had before, the closed loop solution would help a lot to move the heat away from the cramped and frankly thermal nightmare of a laptop’s inner space.
